title: The Ridgeline Report
region: Upper Hudson headwaters, southwestern Adirondacks, New York
reported_by: Volunteer trail steward, Beaver Meadow lean-to
briefing:
A trail steward checking the snow-melt drainage east of camp reported 'a big cat, grey, with black ear tufts and huge feet' crossing the old logging track at first light. She had no camera. She was certain it was not a bobcat.

That report on its own is worth very little. Bobcats are common in this valley and are routinely reported as lynx, especially at low light and at distance. Tracks in soft ground spread and read larger than the animal that made them.

There is at least one bobcat using this drainage. There may also be a lynx. Both leave four-toed, clawless prints in the same mud, and from ten metres away a trail of one looks much like a trail of the other.

So do not go looking for an animal. Go looking for TRACKS, and let them tell you which animal to follow. A lynx print is roughly twice the width of a bobcat's, rounder, and blurred at the edges by the fur on its feet. Measure what you find. When the measurements start pointing one way, follow that trail and not the other.

Scenario note: the setting and the report are written for this game. The species information, conservation status and tracking characteristics in your field guide are drawn from published science. Nothing you conclude in the field here is a real observation record.

objectives.text: Work the creek margins east of camp. Mud holds a print; leaf litter and ledge rock do not.
Measure at least four prints. One track is an accident; a set of measurements is a trail.
Follow the larger prints to the animal that made them, and photograph it well enough to be reviewed. A photograph of the wrong cat is still evidence — it just is not this.
Build a case broad enough to be worth filing. Repeats of one kind of sign count for little.
File your determination. Inconclusive is a legitimate result.
